newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems return to village in Serb territory.
newsitem.headline: Moslems return to village in Serb territory.

text.p: Some 60 jubilant Moslem refugees returned to their ruined village in Bosnian Serb- controlled territory on Sunday without incident under rules set down by international mediators.
Russian and U.S. peacekeeping troops patrolled the area as the group moved in accompanied by hundreds of fellow Moslems who lent a helping hand.
"I feel like never before in my life. After four years I am returning to my village," Zejnil Latifovic, 20, said. "This means a lot to me."

Some 100 Moslem men moved back to Jusici last month but Russian troops discovered some of them were carrying submachine guns and grenades in territory that lies inside the so-called "zone of separation", which is banned under the Dayton peace accord.

NATO and international mediators persuaded the Moslems to move out for three days to allow for a registration procedure to ensure that those returning had documents proving they were pre-war residents.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNCHR) received 117 applications and had approved 60 in time for Sunday, relief officials said.

The Dayton peace accord guarantees refugees the right to return to their homes. But nationalist authorities have prevented people from crossing former front lines in a bid to preserve the results of wartime "ethnic cleansing".
Officers in the NATO-led peace force (IFOR) and Western mediators were keen to defuse the tensions surrounding Jusici without discouraging displaced people from moving back to their homes.
Russian and U.S. troops stationed nearby patrolled the area to ensure neither the Moslems or Serbs brought in weapons.
The Moslems were jubilant to be coming home even though most of their homes were destroyed or heavily damaged by 3-1/2 years of war.
Before entering Jusici, the village mayor, Nekir Islamovic, urged the Moslems to cooperate if they met any Serb police.
"If there are Serb police in the village behave yourself and be hospitable," Islamovic said.
At one point, the returning villagers heard that a Serb had killed one of their number and the crowd took up sticks and shovels expecting a fight. But the rumour proved false.
IFOR troops said an elderly Moslem man had fainted when a Russian soldier asked to see his identification.
U.S. General George Casey, who observed the return, said he was satisifed the rules agreed last week for Jusici refugees had worked out well.
"I think we had a good day today. I think we proved to the people that the process works as the (local Moslem authorities) promised and as we promised," Casey told reporters.
IFOR soldiers said they had found unexploded ammunition over the past three days in the village, but it was not clear when the explosives were planted.
